summary: This document describes a DHCPv4 option for exchanging information about a client's fully qualified domain name and about who is responsible for updating the DNS records related to the client's address assignment.

plainLanguage.summary: When a host gets an address by DHCP, the DNS records that map its name to that address, and the address back to its name, have to be updated by somebody. Without an agreed rule, sites end up with stale or conflicting records. This RFC adds a DHCP option that carries the client's domain name and a set of flag bits that tell the server who will do the DNS updates.

questions: who updates dns for dhcp clients
what is the dhcp client fqdn option
what do the s o n e bits mean in client fqdn
subtitle: A DHCP option that carries a client's domain name and says who updates the DNS records for it.

tldr.problem: When a host gets an address by DHCP, the DNS records that map its name to that address, and the address back to its name, have to be updated by somebody. Without an agreed rule, sites end up with stale or conflicting records.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines DHCP option 81, the Client FQDN option, which carries the client's domain name plus four flag bits: S asks the server to update the forward record, N asks it to do no updates at all, O says the server overrode the request, and E says which encoding the name uses.
tldr.outcome: The client and the server agree in one exchange who does the DNS work, and the server's answer states what it will do. The RFC also recommends short TTLs for the records, no more than a third of the lease time, and secure DNS updates.

facts.label: Flag bits
facts.value: S, O, N and E, with the remaining four bits reserved

facts.label: RCODE fields
facts.value: Deprecated: clients set 0, servers set 255, and both ignore them on receipt

facts.label: Suggested TTL
facts.value: No more than one third of the lease time, and no less than 10 minutes

facts.label: Name encodings
facts.value: Canonical wire format, or a deprecated ASCII encoding

today: RFC 4702 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2006, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the specification of the DHCPv4 Client FQDN option, code 81, and IANA was asked to reference this document for that option.

sections.title: The Problem the Option Solves
sections.content:
DNS maintains, among other things, the information about the mapping between hosts' Fully Qualified Domain Names and IP addresses assigned to the hosts. That information is maintained in two types of Resource Records: A and PTR. The DNS update specification describes a mechanism that enables DNS information to be updated over a network.

DHCP provides a mechanism by which a host, a DHCP client, can acquire certain configuration information along with its address. This document specifies a DHCP option, the Client FQDN option, which can be used by DHCP clients and servers to exchange information about the client's fully qualified domain name for an address, and about who has the responsibility for updating the DNS with the associated A and PTR records.

When a DHCP client acquires a new address, a site's administrator may desire that one or both of the A record for the client's FQDN and the PTR record for the acquired address be updated. Acquiring an address involves two entities, a client and a server, and in principle each could perform none, one or both of the two update transactions. In practice the option is primarily intended for two cases: the client updates the A record and the server updates the PTR record, or the server updates both. The only difference is whether the FQDN-to-address mapping is updated by the client or by the server; the address-to-FQDN mapping is updated by the server in both cases.

The reason these two cases matter is authority over the DNS domain names. A client may be given authority over mapping its own A records, or that authority may be restricted to a server to prevent the client from listing arbitrary addresses or associating its address with arbitrary domain names. In all cases, the only reasonable place for the authority over the PTR records associated with the address is in the DHCP server that allocates the address. A third case is supported, where the client asks the server to perform no updates, but this is presumed to be rare because of the authority issues.
sections.plainLanguage: A host that gets its address over DHCP also needs DNS records, one mapping its name to the address and one mapping the address back to the name. The question this RFC answers is who writes them: the host or the server that handed out the address. The answer is carried in the option itself, so both sides know what was agreed.

sections.title: The Format of the Option
sections.content:
To update the IP-address-to-FQDN mapping, a DHCP server needs to know the FQDN of the client to which it leases the address. To allow the client to convey its FQDN to the server, the document defines a new DHCP option, the Client FQDN option. It also contains Flags, which servers can use to convey information about DNS updates to clients, and two deprecated RCODEs.

Clients MAY send the option in both their DHCPDISCOVER and DHCPREQUEST messages. If a client sends it in a DHCPDISCOVER, it MUST send it in subsequent DHCPREQUEST messages, though the contents MAY change. Only one Client FQDN option MAY appear in a message, though it may be instantiated as multiple options, so implementations MUST implement DHCP option concatenation. The code for this option is 81, and Len contains the number of octets that follow it, with a minimum value of 3. The format is Code, Len, Flags, RCODE1, RCODE2 and then the Domain Name.

The two 1-octet RCODE1 and RCODE2 fields are deprecated. A client SHOULD set these to 0 when sending the option and SHOULD ignore them on receipt; a server SHOULD set them to 255 when sending and MUST ignore them on receipt. They were originally used by a server to report the response code from any A or PTR update it had performed, or 255 to mean an update had been started but not completed. They predate EDNS0, which extends the length of a DNS RCODE to 12 bits, and that is another reason to deprecate them. A client that needs to confirm that the update has been done MAY use a DNS query, but depending on server load and DNS propagation delays it can only infer success.
sections.plainLanguage: The option has a fixed number of bytes: a code of 81, a length, one byte of flags, two bytes that are kept only for compatibility and should be ignored, and then the name itself. A client may send it in both the discover and the request messages, and if it sends it in the discover it must send it in the request too, although the name inside may change.

sections.title: The Four Flag Bits
sections.content:
The Flags field is one octet, with the top four bits marked MBZ and the low four bits labelled N, E, O and S.

The S bit indicates whether the server SHOULD or SHOULD NOT perform the A record, the FQDN-to-address, DNS updates. A client sets it to 0 to say the server should not and 1 to say it should. The state of the bit in the server's reply indicates the action the server has taken; if it is 1, the server has taken responsibility for the A record updates.

The O bit indicates whether the server has overridden the client's preference for the S bit. A client MUST set it to 0, and a server MUST set it to 1 if the S bit in its reply does not match the S bit it received.

The N bit indicates whether the server SHOULD NOT perform any DNS updates. A client sets it to 0 to request that the server should perform updates, the PTR record and possibly the A record depending on the S bit, or to 1 to request that the server should perform none. A server sets it to say whether it shall or shall not perform DNS updates. If the N bit is 1, the S bit MUST be 0.

The E bit indicates the encoding of the Domain Name field. 1 indicates canonical wire format without compression, which clients SHOULD use and servers MUST support. 0 indicates a now-deprecated ASCII encoding. A server MUST use the same encoding as the client, and a server that does not support the deprecated ASCII encoding MUST ignore options that use it. The remaining MBZ bits MUST be cleared by senders and ignored by receivers.
sections.plainLanguage: Four bits in the flags carry the decision. S says whether the server should write the name-to-address record. N says whether the server should write no DNS records at all. O is the server saying that it did something other than what was asked. E says which encoding the name uses.

sections.title: How the Name Is Carried
sections.content:
The Domain Name part of the option carries all or part of the FQDN of a DHCP client. The data SHOULD appear in canonical wire format. If the client uses canonical wire format, it MUST set the E bit to 1. In order to determine whether the FQDN has changed between message exchanges, the client and server MUST NOT alter the Domain Name field contents unless the FQDN has actually changed.

A client MAY be configured with a fully qualified domain name or with a partial name that is not fully qualified. If it knows only part of its name, it MAY send a name that is not fully qualified, indicating that it knows part of the name but does not necessarily know the zone in which the name is to be embedded. To send a fully qualified domain name, the field is set to the DNS-encoded name including the terminating zero-length label; to send a partial name, the terminating zero-length label is omitted. A client MAY also leave the field empty if it desires the server to provide a name.

A substantial population of clients implemented an earlier draft of the specification, which permitted an ASCII encoding of the Domain Name field. Servers SHOULD be aware that clients sending the option with the E bit set to 0 are using ASCII, and MAY be prepared to return an ASCII-encoded version. Servers that are not prepared to return one MUST ignore the option if the E bit is 0. The use of ASCII encoding in this option SHOULD be considered deprecated.
sections.plainLanguage: The name is carried in the DNS wire format, with a bit that says so. A client may send the whole name, part of it, or nothing at all if it wants the server to choose one. An older ASCII encoding is still out there, so servers have to check the bit and ignore the option if they cannot handle it.

sections.title: What the Client Does
sections.content:
The client behaviour depends on which of the three roles it wants. If a client that owns and maintains its own FQDN wants to be responsible for updating the FQDN-to-address mapping, it MUST include the option in its DHCPREQUEST, and it MAY include it in its DHCPDISCOVER, with the S, O and N bits all 0. Once its DHCP configuration is completed, the client MAY originate an update for the A record unless the server has set the S bit to 1. A client that is explicitly configured with an FQDN MAY ignore the state of the S bit if the server's returned name matches its configured name.

If the client wants the server to do the updates, it SHOULD include the option in its DHCPREQUEST and MAY include it in its DHCPDISCOVER, with the S bit 1 and the O and N bits 0. If the client wants the server to do no updates at all, it again SHOULD include the option in its DHCPREQUEST and MAY include it in its DHCPDISCOVER, with the N bit 1 and the S and O bits 0. Once the configuration is completed, the client MAY originate its own DNS updates provided the server's N bit is 1; if the server's N bit is 0, the server MAY perform the PTR updates and may also perform the A updates if the S bit is 1.

Because the server may complete or replace a domain name that the client sends, the client MAY find it useful to send the option in its DHCPDISCOVER. If the server returns different Domain Name data in its DHCPOFFER, the client could use that data in its own eventual A record update, or in the option it sends in its DHCPREQUEST. There is no requirement that the client send identical data in the two messages, and a client whose configuration changes may send the new name data when it next communicates with the server.

A client that delegates the responsibility for updating the mapping to a server will not receive any indication, positive or negative, of whether the server was able to perform the update, so it MAY use a DNS query to check. If a client releases its lease before it expires and is responsible for updating its A record, it SHOULD delete that record before sending the DHCPRELEASE message, and a client that cannot delete an A record it added because it has lost the use of its address SHOULD attempt to notify its administrator, perhaps by emitting a log message. A client that desires to perform DNS updates to A records SHOULD NOT do so if its address is a private address. Clients that send the Client FQDN option MUST NOT also send the Host Name option.
sections.plainLanguage: The client states its choice in the flags. If it owns its name it keeps the S and N bits at zero and updates the name record itself once the lease is confirmed. If it wants the server to do the work it sets the S bit. If it wants the server to do nothing it sets the N bit. The client must not send the older host name option as well, and it should remove its own name record when it gives the address back.

sections.title: What the Server Does
sections.content:
The server examines its configuration and the flag bits in the client's option to determine how to respond. If the client's E bit is 0 and the server does not support ASCII encoding, the server SHOULD ignore the option. The server sets to 0 the S, O and N bits in its copy of the option, and copies the client's E bit. If the client's N bit is 1 and the server's configuration allows it to honour that request, the server sets the N bit to 1. Otherwise, if the client's S bit is 1 and the server's configuration allows it to honour that request, the server sets the S bit to 1, and if that bit does not match the client's S bit, the server sets the O bit to 1.

The server MAY be configured to use the name supplied in the client's option, to modify it, or to substitute a different name, and SHOULD send its notion of the complete FQDN in the Domain Name field. It MUST use the same encoding format that the client used and MUST set the E bit accordingly. If a client sends both the Client FQDN and Host Name options, the server SHOULD ignore the Host Name option. The server SHOULD set RCODE1 and RCODE2 to 255 before sending the option in a DHCPOFFER or DHCPACK.

The server SHOULD NOT perform any DNS updates if the N bit is 1 in the option in the DHCPACK, but it SHOULD delete any records that it previously added for the client. It MAY perform the PTR update unless the N bit is 1, and it MAY perform the A update if the S bit is 1. It MAY perform these updates even if the client's DHCPREQUEST did not carry the option, but it MUST NOT initiate DNS updates when responding to DHCPDISCOVER messages. It MAY perform the updates before or after sending the DHCPACK. If the server's A record update does not complete until after it has replied to the client, its interaction with the DNS server may cause it to change the domain name it associates with the client, so the name the server returns could change between two DHCP exchanges. When a lease expires, the server SHOULD delete any PTR record it added, and if it added an A record on the client's behalf it SHOULD delete that too. The same applies when the server terminates a lease early, for instance by sending a DHCPNAK.
sections.plainLanguage: The server looks at the flags and at its own configuration, and then answers with flags that state what it will actually do. If it does something other than the client asked, it sets the O bit. The server owns the reverse mapping, so it is the one that writes the PTR record, and it may also write the name record if the client asked it to. It must never update DNS while answering a discover message, only when it hands out the address, and it must clean up the records it added when the lease ends.

sections.title: TTL Values and Name Conflicts
sections.content:
Records associated with DHCP clients may be more volatile than statically configured records. Clients and servers that perform dynamic updates should try to specify TTLs that reflect this volatility, in order to minimize the possibility that a DNS answer returns a record referring to an address assignment that has expired or been released. The RFC suggests that the TTLs for records added as a result of DHCP activity SHOULD be less than the initial lease time, that the TTL SHOULD NOT exceed one third of the lease time, and that it SHOULD NOT be less than 10 minutes. Administrators should be able to configure TTLs and their bounds, either as an absolute interval or as a percentage of the lease time.

The document does not resolve how a client or server prevents name conflicts. It addresses only how the client and server negotiate who will perform the DNS updates and which fully qualified domain name is used. Implementers will need to consider how conflicts are prevented: if a DNS updater needs a security token to perform updates on a specific name, conflicts can only occur if multiple updaters are given that token; if the fully qualified domains are based on the specific address bound to a client, conflicts will not occur; or a name conflict resolution technique SHOULD be used.
sections.plainLanguage: Records for DHCP clients go stale quickly, so they should carry short lifetimes. The RFC suggests a TTL of no more than a third of the lease time and no less than ten minutes. It does not settle the name-conflict question, only who does the updates and which name is used.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Unauthenticated updates to the DNS can lead to tremendous confusion, through malicious attack or through inadvertent misconfiguration, and administrators need to be wary of permitting unsecured DNS updates to zones exposed to the global Internet. Both DHCP clients and servers should use some form of update request origin authentication procedure, such as Secure DNS Dynamic Update, when performing DNS updates.

Whether the client or the server is responsible for updating the FQDN-to-IP-address mapping is a site-local matter, likely based on the security model used with the DNS update protocol: only a client may have sufficient credentials to update the mapping for its own FQDN. Whether the server always updates the mapping regardless of the wishes of an individual client is also a site-local matter. In cases where the server performs updates on behalf of a client, it should be sure of the DNS name to use for the client and of the identity of the client.

It is currently difficult for DHCP servers to develop much confidence in the identity of their clients, given the absence of entity authentication from the DHCP protocol itself. If DHCP Authentication becomes widely deployed, this may become more customary. One situation that offers extra assurances is when the client is connected through a cable modem termination system, where MAC address spoofing does not occur. Another is a configuration where clients obtain network access through a network access server using PPP, where the server may be obtaining addresses by DHCP and encoding a client identification into the DHCP client-id option. It is critical to implement proper conflict resolution, and the security considerations of conflict resolution apply.
sections.plainLanguage: Updating DNS without checking who is asking can cause a lot of confusion, so both sides should authenticate their update requests. Which side does the updating is a local policy decision, usually driven by which side holds the credentials the DNS requires. The RFC also notes that a DHCP server has little way of knowing who a client really is, because DHCP itself does not authenticate the client.

fields.name: Len
fields.desc: The number of octets that follow, with a minimum value of 3.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: One octet holding the MBZ bits and the N, E, O and S bits.

fields.name: RCODE1
fields.desc: Deprecated. Clients set it to 0 and servers to 255, and both ignore it.

fields.name: RCODE2
fields.desc: Deprecated. Clients set it to 0 and servers to 255, and both ignore it.

fields.name: Domain Name
fields.desc: All or part of the client's FQDN, in canonical wire format unless the E bit says otherwise.

viz.caption: THE FOUR FLAG BITS OF THE OPTION

items.label: Server updates the A record
items.desc: The client sets it to 1 to ask the server to update the name-to-address record. A set bit in the reply means the server has taken that responsibility.

items.label: No server updates
items.desc: The client sets it to 1 to ask the server to perform no DNS updates at all. If it is 1, the S bit must be 0.

items.label: Server overrode the client
items.desc: The server sets it to 1 when its S bit does not match the S bit it received. Clients always set it to 0.

items.label: Encoding of the name
items.desc: 1 means canonical wire format without compression, 0 means the deprecated ASCII encoding.

viz.caption: THE THREE ROLES A CLIENT CAN ASK FOR

cells: The client updates the A record
The client, the server updates the PTR record
The client, if it wants to
